newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch moot Euro-U.S summit on east Europe aid.
newsitem.headline: Dutch moot Euro-U.S summit on east Europe aid.

text.p: Dutch Prime Minister Wim Kok paid tribute on Wednesday to the United States for its Marshall Plan to rebuild Europe 50 years ago, and said the Dutch may hold a similar Euro-Atlantic initiative on eastern Europe.

"With the Cold War now relegated to history, we have a great opportunity to continue the process that George Marshall and true Europeans...initiated 50 years ago," Kok said in a speech released ahead of delivery.
The Dutch premier was due later to address a celebratory gathering of European and North American leaders in The Hague.
The Netherlands was willing to host a transatlantic conference later this year to thrash out ways of helping the flow of funds to central and eastern Europe, he said.

U.S President Bill Clinton, among three dozen leaders attending 50th anniversary celebrations of the Marshall Plan, earlier pledged to work closer with the European Union to step up efforts to revive the economies of the former Communist bloc.
Clinton said he expected "a new set of initiatives that meet the demands of this time" and having a similar impact to that of the Marshall Plan.
Kok said that while economic growth in central and eastern Europe was "clearly evident", assistance to their economies was still needed on a massive scale.
"Estimates of the funds needed run as high as $100 billion," he said. "If only because of the sheer magnitude of these needs, most of the money will have to come from private investment."
It was for European countries and their North American partners to look for ways to ease the path for private capital to the former Soviet bloc states, he said.

Co-financing and providing for investment guarantees were the right avenues to be explored, Kok told heads of the Organisation of Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) at a ceremony in the medieval surrounds of the Dutch parliament.

"If we are prepared to shoulder this responsibility, we will all reap the benefits, as was the case in the Marshall era," Kok added. "Let us build a European house for all -- this time let no-one who is ready to join be left out."
The current Dutch EU presidency hopes to broker a Treaty of Amsterdam at a summit in June, paving the way for eastern European nations to join the 15-member alliance.
Between 1948-1952, the United States poured over $12 billion of aid to 16 European countries to help them rebuild their shattered industries and stave off hunger and instability.

Soviet dictator Joseph Stalin did not allow Marshall Aid to be distributed to Eastern Europe, where living standards fell far behind those in the West as the region remained under communist rule for almost half a century after the war.
